newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: FEATURE - Cambodia rebels want to cash in on gems.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Cambodia rebels want to cash in on gems.

text.p: Rubies and sapphires are sprinkled everywhere -- in the soil of the streets, beneath the modest houses and in the pockets of children who pluck them up in idle moments.
In this stronghold of dissident Khmer Rouge rebels in northwest Cambodia, Ranin, 33, casually hands over a plastic bag with about 20 rough blue and red stones.
In impoverished Cambodia, Pailin is a land of plenty, and eager entrepreneurs are ready to transform this bitterly contested battlegound into a business bonanza.
Dissident guerrillas and villagers say about 200 Thai merchants regularly commute to Pailin to operate 20 gem mines around the town, generating the funds that have kept years of civil war simmering.
"The gem mines are all Thai companies," said Kun Kamra, 45, commander of a battalion in Pailin.
But now that peace and profiteering have come to Pailin, the Thai monopoly on the area could soon end, say military analysts.

Khmer Rouge guerrillas loyal to dissident leader Ieng Sary agreed at the weekend to merge their forces with the government, and rebels told Reuters they are free to own and sell land. Ieng Sary broke with hardliners in August to force the peace sttlement with the govermnment.

Powerful businessman Teng Boonma, president of the Phnom Penh Chamber of Commerce, travelled to Pailin with co-Premier Hun Sen on October 22, along with Malaysian businessmen, a spokesman for the second prime minister said.
A Cambodian-Canadian businessman who gave only the name Lang said he was making his third trip to Pailin and said there was plenty of gem- and timber-rich land for the asking.
"People will sell their land, and the government says it will honour the contracts," Lang said, adding that he knew of 30 Cambodians who were in talks with Pailin land owners.
As he spoke, Khmer Rouge dissidents, government soldiers, children and villagers were combing a public field across the street for sapphires and rubies.
Kun Kamra said many villagers were considering selling concessions to their land. They planned to collect money in exchange for allowing business people to extract gems.
He thought some of the 25- by 50-metre plots allotted to each family could fetch up to 30,000 baht ($1,200) for concessions.

The potential for a free-for-all worries officials at the Ministry of Industry, Mines and Energy. A top official who asked to remain anonymous said the ministry has virtually no control over the situation, despite its mandate to regulate gem mining.
The unbridled capitalism shows how strongly this breakaway town has rejected the ideology of Pol Pot, who led the brutal 1975-1979 regime that killed more than one million Cambodians.
"Pol Pot wanted us to all be poor farmers," said Kun Kamra, noting that Pol Pot had recently removed the hammer from the hammer-and-sickle logo of the Khmer Rouge to underline the message.
"But we want to own our land and have businesses," he added.
